title: Equals means same value
goal: Read the equals sign as “has the same value as.”
text: An equals sign is a promise: the amount on the left is exactly the amount on the right. It does not mean “the answer comes next.”
steps: Evaluate each side separately. Both have value five.
Both sides have value five, even though they look different.
Five is not six. An equation can be false.
note: You can read an equation either way: 5 = 3 + 2 is just as true as 3 + 2 = 5.

check.hint: Both sides must have value seven.
steps: Both sides must have value seven.

school: The left side makes 7. The two parts on the right must also make 7.
The missing part is 7 − 5 = 2. Put 2 in the box.
algebra: Later we can name the same missing number x: 3 + 4 = x + 5.
7 = x + 5. Subtract 5 from BOTH sides: 7 − 5 = x + 5 − 5.
bridge.connection: A box and a letter can name the same missing number. Today, focus on the equal values; we will practice the subtract-from-both-sides step in episode 4.

title: Keep it balanced
goal: Change an equation without breaking its promise.
text: If two amounts are equal, adding the same number to each keeps them equal. Subtracting the same number from each works too.
steps: Take away two from each side.
Equal again. The amounts changed, but the equality stayed true.
note: Adding five to both sides is one action. Reordering a sum is a different idea. Predict what a move will do before you apply it.
ask: Why is adding two to just one side different?

check.q: Start with 6 = 6. Subtract 1 from both sides.
check.hint: 5 = 5; use the same operation and amount.
steps: 5 = 5; use the same operation and amount.

school: The whole is 7. One part is 2 and the other is unknown.
Remove the known part: 7 − 2 = 5. The box is 5.
algebra: Name the missing part x: x + 2 = 7.
bridge.connection: In the bar, removing the known part finds the missing part. In the equation, subtracting 2 from both sides leaves that same missing part. This is a preview; you will control these moves in episode 4.

title: Meet the mystery
goal: Use a letter to stand for a number.
text: A letter can hold a place for a number we want to find. In one problem, every x stands for the same number. A new problem may use a different number.
steps: Three plus two is five. Now we know the mystery number.
Check: put five where x was.
The two sides match. Five works!
note: x names a number, not an object or the multiplication sign ×. In one problem, every x has the same value.
ask: If x = 1, is 2 + x = 3 true? Explain your check.

check.hint: Replace x with six to check.
steps: Replace x with six to check.

school: The unknown whole contains parts 3 and 2.
Add the parts: 3 + 2 = 5. The box is 5.
algebra: Use x instead of the box: x = 3 + 2.
Add the numbers on the right: x = 5.
bridge.connection: We changed the name of the missing number, not the problem. Here x is already alone; there is no need to subtract anything from both sides.

title: Undo addition
goal: Leave x on its own by subtracting from both sides.
text: In 2 + x = 3, the mystery number has two added to it. To uncover x, undo that addition. Subtract two from both sides.
steps: On the left, adding two and subtracting two undo each other. On the right, three minus two is one.
Check the answer in the original equation. It works!
note: The equations 2 + x = 3, x + 2 = 3, and 3 = x + 2 all have the same answer. Zero can be an answer too: 2 + x = 2 gives x = 0.
ask: Would subtracting one from both sides still keep the equation true? Would x be alone yet?

check.hint: Subtract two from both sides. Zero is allowed.
steps: Subtract two from both sides. Zero is allowed.

school: The whole is 3. The known part is 2.
algebra: Name the missing part x: 2 + x = 3.
bridge.connection: The bar method subtracts the known part from the whole. Algebra writes why the same subtraction works: the added 2 and subtracted 2 cancel on the left.
bridge.check: 2 + 1 = 3. The missing part is 1 in both methods.

title: Undo subtraction
goal: Undo taking away by adding to both sides.
text: A mystery starting amount loses three counters and leaves four. To find the starting amount, put three back. In the equation, add three to BOTH sides.
steps: Taking away three and adding three undo each other.
Check the original equation. Seven works.
note: Choose the opposite of the operation on x. Do not always subtract the visible number.
ask: Why would subtracting three again fail to uncover the starting amount?

school: The missing number is the starting whole. Its parts are 3 taken away and 4 left.
Put the parts together: 3 + 4 = 7. The box is 7.
algebra: Name the starting whole x: x − 3 = 4.
bridge.connection: This time we need the whole, not a missing part. The picture joins the parts; algebra undoes subtraction by adding. Do not automatically subtract the number you see.

title: Equal groups
goal: Read 2x as two equal amounts and solve by sharing.
text: Two bags hold the same number of counters. Together they hold eight. Use x for the number in EACH bag.
steps: Two copies of x make eight.
2x is a shorter way to write 2 × x. Pause here: explain what 2x means.
Share both sides into two equal parts.
Each bag holds four counters. Check: 2 × 4 = 8.
note: Equal-looking bags need not hold equal amounts. Here the STORY tells us the amounts match. At x = 3, 2x is 6 but x + 2 is 5.
ask: What does 3x mean? Solve 3x = 12. Pause before division if the notation is still new.

check.hint: Share twelve into three equal amounts.
steps: Share twelve into three equal amounts.

bridge.problem: Two equal boxes hold 8 counters altogether.
school: The story says the two parts are equal. Share 8 into 2 equal parts.
algebra: Let x be the count in EACH box: x + x = 8, or 2x = 8.
bridge.connection: Each equal part is one x. Sharing the whole equally is the picture version of dividing both sides. Two boxes do not always mean equal numbers; this story tells us they match.

title: Use what you know
goal: Replace a letter with its known value.
text: Substitution means putting a known number in place of its letter. Here we know x. That helps us find B.
steps: Replace x with three. Keep everything else the same.
These are two different letters with their own values. Check: five really is two plus three.
note: x is known; B is the number to find. Different letters CAN have equal values. B = x + 3 alone allows many pairs: (1,4) and (2,5), for example.
ask: With x = 4 and B = x + 3, which number is known? Which must you find?

check.q: x = 4 and B = x + 3. Find B.
check.hint: x is known; replace it with four.
steps: x is known; replace it with four.

title: Undo two steps
goal: Undo the extra amount, then share equal groups.
text: Two bags hold equal numbers of counters. Three loose counters sit beside them. Altogether there are eleven. Find the number in each bag.
steps: The two equal bags hold eight altogether.
Check the original equation, including the extra three.
note: A legal move keeps equality true. A useful move also helps uncover x. If you divide first, divide EVERY term: (2x + 4) ÷ 2 = 12 ÷ 2 becomes x + 2 = 6.
ask: Solve 2x + 5 = 13. Why remove five before sharing?

check.hint: Subtract five, then divide by two.
steps: Subtract five, then divide by two.

title: Translate “more than”
goal: Turn a comparison into an equation.
text: There are five more adults than children. A is the NUMBER of adults; C is the NUMBER of children. Start with C, then add five to find A.
steps: One possible pair is three children and eight adults.
Another pair is four children and nine adults.
Both pairs have five more adults. Without a total, we cannot choose just one pair.
note: The larger count has the extra part. “Two more blue beads than red beads” means B = R + 2, not R = B + 2.
ask: Which count is larger? Where is the extra part in a bar picture?

check.q: Two more blue beads than red. There are 3 red beads. Find blue.

title: Two clues, two quantities
goal: Translate a story into a picture and two equations.
text: There are five more adults than children in a room. There are thirteen people altogether. How many adults and how many children?
steps: A is the adult count; C is the child count. Replace the whole A with C + 5.
C + C is two equal groups of C. We write that as 2C.
Subtract the five extra adults from both sides.
Divide both sides by two. There are four children.
Check BOTH clues: thirteen total and five more adults.
note: First solve using matching bars and check both clues. Pause if needed. Then replace the WHOLE A with (C + 5). Each matching bar is a C-sized amount; one is children and one is an equal number of adults.
ask: Find the counts for four more blue beads than red and sixteen beads altogether. Check the total AND difference.

check.q: Four more blue beads than red, sixteen altogether. Find both.

title: Choose a method and check
goal: Choose your own operation and explain why it works.
text: Look carefully at what has happened to x. Choose an undoing operation, apply it to both sides, then check your answer in the original problem.
steps: Undo addition by subtracting three from both sides.
Adding three to eight would give eleven, but eleven fails the check.
note: Use counters, a drawing, words, or equations to explain. A correct answer with a hint is useful practice; a fresh unprompted explanation gives different evidence.
ask: How would your method change for x − 4 = 3 or 2x = 10?

check.hint: Subtract one, divide by two, check.
steps: Subtract one, divide by two, check.

title: Optional: answer detective
goal: Check the arithmetic AND the meaning of an answer.
text: Five more adults than children, twelve people altogether: remove the five extras. Can the remaining seven people split into two equal whole-number counts?
steps: Seven cannot split into two equal whole-number groups
One counter is left after making two groups of three.
Both clues cannot hold for counts of whole people.
If you know halves: C = 3.5, A = 8.5
These numbers fit the equations but not whole-person counts.
note: This is an optional extension. Fractions can describe juice or length; they cannot count whole people in this story. With four extras and twelve total, C = 4 and A = 8 works.
ask: Would twelve people work if there were FOUR more adults than children?

check.q: Four more adults than children and twelve people. Whole-person answer possible?
